planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings after the last frost on a sturdy trellis in a warm, sheltered site, since this vine is less cold-hardy than arguta or kolomikta kiwi.

directions: This vigorous twining liana from the Himalayas and southern China/Taiwan bears small, smooth-skinned, yellow-green fruit that is edible but milder and less prized than commercial kiwifruit, making it mostly a collector's or breeding plant rather than a market crop. Like other kiwi species it is dioecious, so both a male and female vine are needed for fruit set, and it wants a strong permanent trellis since top growth is extremely vigorous once established. It tolerates more heat and less winter cold than hardy kiwi, so it suits mild-winter gardens where arguta and kolomikta kiwi struggle. Prune annually in dormancy to keep fruiting wood within reach and improve airflow.

planting.note: Plant on a strong trellis in a sheltered spot after the last frost, pairing a male vine with females since the species is dioecious.

directions: Native to south-central China, this species is a parent of modern gold-fleshed kiwifruit cultivars and is prized for fruit with notably bright, vitamin-rich flesh under a soft, easily-rubbed-off fuzzy skin. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than hardy kiwi (A. arguta), so give it wind protection and a warm exposure in marginal zones. Fruit is smaller and rounder than supermarket kiwifruit but ripens with excellent sweetness where summers are long and warm. Train young vines onto a permanent trellis or pergola early, since mature plants become heavy and widespread.

planting.note: Grow on a trellis or arbor where the brilliant red-woolly young stems and petioles can be seen up close; needs a male and female vine for fruit.

directions: This central Chinese kiwi relative is grown as much for ornament as for fruit, since its young stems, leaf stalks, and flower buds are covered in a dense, brilliant red woolly pubescence that stands out dramatically against the foliage. The egg-shaped, softly fuzzy brownish fruit is edible and sweet once fully ripe, though yields are modest compared to commercial kiwi species. Give it the same dioecious pairing and sturdy trellising as other Actinidia, and site it where the colorful new growth will be visible from a distance. It performs well in part shade in hot climates, unlike most other kiwi species which prefer full sun.

planting.note: Site on a sturdy trellis in a cool, humid mountain-garden setting reminiscent of its native Japanese woodland habitat.

directions: Native to the mountains of Japan, this deciduous twining vine produces fragrant white flowers followed by smooth, yellowish, edible fruit, and is grown mainly by kiwi enthusiasts and breeders rather than commercial growers. It tolerates cooler, shadier woodland-edge conditions better than most other kiwi species, making it useful for gardeners without a full-sun trellis site. As with all Actinidia, separate male and female vines are required for fruit set. Keep soil consistently moist and slightly acidic, mimicking the humid montane forests where it naturally grows.

planting.note: Plant in a warm, sheltered coastal-climate garden; the reddish-rust hairs on new stems give this species its name and help distinguish it from similar-looking A. arguta.

directions: Found in Japan, Taiwan, and the Ryukyu Islands, this warm-climate kiwi relative closely resembles hardy kiwi but is distinguished by rust-red hairs on its young shoots and a greater tolerance for heat and humidity than cold. Its smooth-skinned fruit is edible and similar in size to kiwiberries, but the plant is grown far more often for its curiosity value among collectors than for fruit production. Provide a sturdy trellis and full sun, and expect less winter dieback than A. arguta only in genuinely mild climates. Dioecious like its relatives, it needs a male pollenizer planted nearby for the females to set fruit.
